name: PT Medikaloka Hermina Tbk

frontmatter.title: Hermina Hospitals: a good franchise priced for a better one
frontmatter.summary: Hermina operates a top-tier private hospital network and still adds two greenfield hospitals a year, but returns on that reinvestment sit below its cost of equity, so growth is not yet creating value. At the current price the market still pays for a re-acceleration the last actual and the company's own plan do not support. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: The franchise is real: a national private hospital network with maternity-led, mid-market positioning and a doctor base that is hard to replicate [S2].
The reinvestment arithmetic does not yet work: capex has run near a quarter of revenue and ROE sits below the cost of equity [S0][S3].
Reported EBITDA understates the depreciation a network of this size carries; on the disclosed margin the shares trade on a fuller multiple than the pack implies [S3].
KRIS and BPJS tariff reform is the swing factor for private-room revenue and is still unresolved in the implementing regulation [S6][S7].
Our blended value sits below the market price; the de-rating from the high is largely deserved.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: first full year of the revised single-digit revenue plan and the test of whether FCF turns
KRIS implementing regulation after the June 2026 harmonisation of the three-class framework
Annual dividend decision; payout has risen every year through the build-out

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Medikaloka Hermina with a **SELL** rating and a target price of **Rp259**, -44.6% total return from Rp490. Hermina operates the Hermina Hospitals network: 42 hospitals in 31 cities across Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, with more than 3,000 beds and about 2,800 affiliated doctors [S2]. It is a genuine franchise with a maternity-led, mid-market positioning that sits between the premium Jakarta operators and the mass BPJS hospitals.

The variant view is not about demand. It is about the price of growth. Hermina has spent between a fifth and a third of revenue on capex in each of the last four years, borrowed to do it, and the resulting return on equity (6.9%) is below our cost of equity (12.3%). When a company reinvests at a return below its cost of capital, growth subtracts value per share, however impressive the top line looks. On our numbers the group converts almost none of its EBITDA into free cash flow while the current slate is being built: free cash flow to the firm is a thin IDR11.1bn on IDR1,737.7bn of EBITDA in FY2026E, IDR146.9bn in FY2027E and IDR239.1bn in FY2028E, a conversion in the low teens at best, and the capex ratio is set to hold near 16.0% of revenue rather than fall back to the D&A charge [S0][S3]. Cash returns, not negative cash, are the point: the build consumes almost all the operating cash the network generates.

The second thing that moves the value is the margin line. FY2025 was the first year in four in which gross margin fell, and the third quarter of 2025 was weaker again, as medical inflation and a weaker rupiah raised the cost of imported drugs and devices faster than tariffs could be reset [S3]. Management cut its 2026 revenue plan to single-digit growth on 9 November 2026, reduced its 2030 hospital target and re-phased 2027 capex toward acquisitions and medical equipment [S8], and the twelve months to September 2026, which the pack reports directly, show revenue growth of a few percent with net profit attributable down on the prior twelve months [S0][S8]. Our FY2026E reproduces that: revenue growth of 5.0% and net profit of IDR401.1bn, below FY2025A, with the operating margin held at the LTM's 12.0% EBIT margin rather than a recovery. That is a deceleration, not a collapse, but it is the opposite of the compounding story the shares were priced for at the high.

The third is regulation. The KRIS standard for inpatient rooms, mandated by Perpres 59/2024 with a mid-2025 deadline, is still being implemented through a three-class framework harmonised in June 2026, and the Ministry of Health says 60.9% of hospitals meet the criteria [S6][S7]. For a private operator with a large JKN-covered book, how the classes and tariffs are finally set is the largest swing factor in revenue per bed [S6].

What the market prices is a franchise that de-rates further only if returns keep falling. What we think is that the de-rating from the fifty-two-week high has done most of the work, but not all of it: on a discounted cash flow basis the equity is worth materially less than the market capitalisation, and the multiple support that would justify today's price rests on an EBITDA line that our own restatement shows is understated by the data pack [S0][S3].

Indonesian private hospitals compete on doctor networks, location density and payer mix. The listed comparables are Mitra Keluarga, Siloam and smaller regional operators; all have de-rated as JKN tariff discipline and medical inflation compressed margins. Hermina's mid-market positioning gives it more JKN exposure than the premium operators, which is both its volume advantage and its tariff risk.

Hermina is a hospital operator, not a healthcare conglomerate. Revenue comes from inpatient and outpatient services, diagnostic support, pharmacy and specialist clinics, all delivered through a single-brand network. The company began in 1985 as a maternity hospital in Jakarta founded by Mrs. Hermina Sulaiman, and the foundation she established still frames the group's positioning in women's and children's health [S2]. The network now runs 42 hospitals in 31 cities across Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi with more than 3,000 beds and around 2,800 affiliated doctors [S2].

**Segments and mix.** Hermina reports as a single hospital-operating segment in the disclosures we have, so we do not have a clean split between inpatient, outpatient and pharmacy revenue. What we can say is that the model is bed-led: revenue per bed is driven by occupancy, case mix and the tariff schedule, and the group's mid-market positioning means a larger share of its patients are JKN-covered than at the premium Jakarta operators. That is the source of both its volume and its tariff sensitivity [S6].

**Strategy.** Management's stated plan is two greenfield hospitals a year, supplemented by acquisitions of hospitals that already have positive operating performance. The CEO has been explicit that the group does not want to be financially burdened by acquisitions, and that greenfield remains the primary route [S3]. Funding for the current slate comes from internal cash, the dividend stream and a treasury capital injection of Rp1,000 IDR bn that closed the buyback overhang [S3].

**Footprint and position.** Hermina is a national challenger rather than the premium leader. Its density is strongest in Greater Jakarta and the secondary cities of Java, where it competes with regional private operators and the public hospital system. On hospital count it is among the largest listed private networks in Indonesia; on revenue per bed it is a mid-market operator [S2].

**Group and controlling shareholder.** The controlling shareholder is the Djarum group. PT Dwimuria Investama Andalan acquired 559 m shares million shares from the buyback at an average of Rp1,875 per share, which removed the treasury stock and brought a large strategic holder onto the register [S3]. Insider ownership is 76.3% and institutional ownership 5.2%; those two alone account for all but a minority of the register, which implies a free float well below the 41.9% the pack's own free-float field reports. Either figure clears the exchange's minimum free-float threshold, so investability is not in question, but the stock is tightly held. The practical consequence is a strategic anchor who bought far above today's price: it reduces the chance of a value-destructive rights issue and concentrates control over capital allocation.

**What the company owns.** Beyond the operating hospitals, the balance sheet carries property, plant and equipment of IDR9,131.4bn, mostly hospital buildings, land and medical equipment [S0]. Minority interests of IDR1,533.2bn reflect the joint-venture structure through which several hospitals are held and which take about a fifth of group net profit [S0]. We treat the JV hospitals as consolidated assets with a minority claim rather than as separate holdings, because that is how the group reports and finances them.

**Demand.** Indonesian private hospital demand is driven by three things: the share of the population covered by JKN, the growth of the urban middle class that buys private rooms, and the epidemiological shift toward chronic and degenerative disease. All three are structurally positive over our horizon, and none of them is the constraint on Hermina's returns. The constraint is price and cost, not volume: the company itself attributed its FY2025 margin fall to higher drug costs and a rising proportion of BPJS patients, which pressed revenue per visit [S3]. JKN is the channel through which both volume and tariff reach the P&L [S6][S7].

**The regulatory driver that matters: KRIS.** Perpres 59/2024 requires hospitals working with BPJS Kesehatan to apply the Kelas Rawat Inap Standar to inpatient facilities, with a deadline of 30 June 2025 [S7]. The implementing framework has since been reworked into three standard classes, harmonised in June 2026, with class A defined as two beds per room with air conditioning, a waiting chair and television; the Deputy Minister of Health said in June 2026 that 60.9% of hospitals already meet the criteria [S6]. Read carefully, these are facilities standards, not a tariff schedule. The same regulation says BPJS continues to pay according to the class entitlement of the participant, and that benefits, tariffs and contributions are to be set separately by 1 July 2025 [S7]; the Deputy Minister told parliament the roll-out is being monitored so that it does "not cause a very large change in cost per case" [S6]. We therefore treat KRIS as an unpriced policy uncertainty that cuts both ways: a standardisation that compresses the premium between the highest and lowest classes would hit revenue per inpatient day for a mid-market operator, while a benefit-package revision that carries a tariff uplift would do the reverse. We do not have a sourced JKN share of Hermina's revenue, so we do not put a number on either direction; what we can source is that the mechanism is tariff-setting, not the facilities rule itself [S6][S7].

**Cost side: medical inflation and the rupiah.** A large share of drugs, devices and consumables is imported or priced off import parity. The macro desk's rupiah path and the current balance-of-payments pressure therefore flow straight into cost of sales with a lag. FY2025 gross margin fell to 33.8% from 36.3% a year earlier, and the third quarter of 2025 was weaker again at the level the company reported [S0][S3]. This is the mechanism behind the compression, and it is why we do not forecast a recovery to the FY2024 level.

**Competitive landscape.** The listed peer set is small: the premium Jakarta operator, the largest national network and several regional players. Hermina's differentiation is mid-market positioning plus maternity and paediatric specialisation, which builds referral relationships with families at first contact. Its weakness is that the same positioning gives it more exposure to JKN tariffs and less pricing power than the premium operators. We do not have a sourced market-share figure for the private hospital market and do not assert one; on bed count Hermina is a top-tier national network, and that is as far as the evidence goes [S2].

**Five forces.** Supplier power is high and rising for medical devices and specialised drugs, which is the medical-inflation channel the company has flagged as its margin driver [S3]. Buyer power is high for the JKN book, where a single payer sets tariffs [S6][S7], and moderate for private patients who choose on doctor and location. Threat of new entry is moderate: a greenfield hospital is capital-intensive but not technologically protected. Rivalry is intensifying in the secondary cities where Hermina is expanding. Substitutes are limited to public hospitals and clinics, which are capacity-constrained.

**Moat assessment.** Hermina has a real but narrow moat. The mechanisms are local density (several hospitals in one catchment sharing specialists and back office), brand trust in maternity and paediatrics, and doctor loyalty built through the group's training and education arm [S2]. None is a switching-cost moat: a patient can change hospital and a doctor can admit elsewhere. That is why we model excess returns fading rather than persisting, and why the terminal value assumes a return on capital only modestly above the cost of capital.

Indonesian hospitals typically engage doctors as independent contractors paid a share of the fees they generate. This keeps fixed costs low but means profitability depends on keeping a roster of high-throughput specialists, and a new hospital needs two to three years to build that roster. It also means reported staff costs understate the true cost of medical labour.

**Revenue build.** Revenue grew from IDR4,901.8bn in FY2022A to IDR7,133.5bn in FY2025A, a compound rate in the mid-teens that masked a sharp deceleration: growth was 18.0% in FY2023A, 16.1% in FY2024A and 6.2% in FY2025A [S0]. The nine-month 2026 figures the pack reports continue at a few percent with attributable profit down on the year, and on 9 November 2026 management cut the 2026 revenue growth plan to single digit and reduced the 2030 hospital target [S8]. Our FY2026E growth of 5.0% reflects that, and we step back up to the high single digits as the two hospitals opened in 2026 and those planned for 2027 add capacity to a base of 42 [S3].

**Margins.** Gross margin peaked at 36.3% in FY2024A and fell to 33.8% in FY2025A; the company reported 33.5% for the third quarter of 2025 with opex at 19.7% of revenue [S0][S3]. The latest actual is better than that on the gross line but worse below it: on the LTM to Sep-2026 the pack shows a gross margin above the FY2025A level while the all-in opex ratio rose to 22.5%, so EBIT margin is 12.0% against 13.2% in FY2025A [S0]. That is the margin structure we carry: FY2026E gross margin at the LTM level, opex at the LTM ratio, and only a modest amount of operating leverage over five years as the 2022-25 cohort matures. Our FY2026E net profit attributable of IDR401.1bn compares with IDR429.5bn in FY2025A, and EPS of Rp26 with Rp28 — consistent with the LTM decline, not a recovery year.

**The D&A restatement — read this before using any multiple.** The data pack reports D&A of IDR279.3bn on revenue of IDR7,133.5bn [S0]. That number is inconsistent with the pack's own balance sheet: property, plant and equipment rose from IDR8,162.7bn at FY2024A to IDR9,131.4bn at FY2025A on capex of IDR1,750.0bn, which leaves depreciation of roughly 11.2% of revenue as the only item that closes the roll-forward [S0]. The company's disclosure agrees: it reported an EBITDA margin of 25.1% and an EBIT margin of 13.8% for the first nine months of 2025, and EBITDA of Rp1,300 IDR bn on revenue of Rp5,300 IDR bn, each of which implies a D&A charge near a tenth of revenue including PSAK 73 right-of-use depreciation [S3]. We model 11.2%, which restates EBITDA up by the difference and is why our EBITDA margin (17.1% in the pack, 23.2% in our forecast) looks discontinuous against history. The discontinuity is a data artefact, not an operating improvement. Note what the restatement does and does not do: EBIT is charged the full all-in opex line, so D&A is a split of EBIT and the FCFF add-back, not an extra cash item. If a reader rejects the restatement and uses the pack's D&A, EBIT is unchanged but the add-back falls by the whole difference, which would cut the DCF by more than half — that is how much the restatement is worth, and it rests on the roll-forward above. Every multiple computed on the pack's EBITDA is treated with suspicion for the same reason.

**Capex and free cash flow.** Capex was IDR1,129.0bn in FY2022A and IDR1,750.0bn in FY2025A, between 24.5% and a third of revenue depending on the year [S0]. The LTM to Sep-2026 is 18.8% of revenue, well below FY2025A, and that is the ratio we carry into FY2026E: the "capex still grows double digits" line in our earlier note was management's 2025 allocation, and FY2025 capex in fact came in below FY2024 [S0][S3]. We model 18.8% of revenue in FY2026E, tapering to 16.0% by FY2030E as the fixed two-hospitals-a-year programme grows only with inflation while the revenue base compounds. On that path free cash flow to the firm turns positive in FY2026E at IDR11.1bn and builds to IDR239.1bn by FY2028E; equity free cash flow is IDR-206.7bn because the dividend takes the rest. The improvement is not a heroic assumption: it is the LTM capex ratio applied to a slightly higher revenue base. The timing question — whether the 2022-25 greenfield cohort maturing in 2027-28 is what lifts return on incremental capital — is the bull case, and the capex peak being already behind us is its strongest evidence [S0].

**Balance sheet and debt.** Net debt was IDR2,497.6bn at FY2025A, 2.0 times reported EBITDA and a little over one times on our restated EBITDA. Interest expense of IDR238.4bn on debt of IDR3,225.4bn is an average coupon near 7.5% — the legacy fixed-rate bank book, well below the 9.4% the WACC charges for new corporate debt [S0]. That gap matters: our P&L build uses the coupon, the discount rate uses the marginal cost, and the difference is a real refinancing risk when the loans roll. We assume no new net borrowing and fund the programme from the cash buffer and the treasury injection. The funding arithmetic: net debt rises from IDR2,497.6bn to a peak of IDR3,399.2bn by FY2028E as the dividend is paid out of a negative FCFE year, then falls as free cash flow turns; cash on the balance sheet is IDR727.8bn at FY2025A. That is covered, but only just, and it is why an equity raise sits in the bear case rather than the base. We could not source the debt covenants or the maturity profile from the documents available and flag that as an open item: a covenant breach is the mechanism by which a funding problem becomes a dilution event.

**Capital allocation and the reinvestment test.** The compounder method card requires the growth rate to be decomposed. Over FY2025A, net reinvestment (capex less D&A plus the working-capital build) was above NOPAT because capex ran at roughly twice our restated depreciation [S0]. With revenue growth in the high single digits, that implies an incremental return on invested capital in the high single digits — at or below our 10.7% WACC. In plain terms: Hermina is not yet earning its cost of capital on the money it puts into new beds. The bull case has to be that this is a timing artefact of immature hospitals; the bear case is that it is structural. We sit between and model a partial improvement through the capex taper.

**Earnings quality flags.** On accruals the group is clean: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025A, and capex of IDR1,750.0bn against EBITDA of IDR1,220.7bn left free cash flow to the firm at IDR-1,072.5bn, so earnings are not outrunning cash even as the balance sheet funds the build [S0]. There are two divergence flags, both optics-class. First, trade receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025A, which we read as slower collection from insurers and BPJS rather than channel stuffing, but we watch it. Second, inventory grew faster than cost of sales as new hospitals stocked up. On structure there is no special-monitoring-board status, no notation letters, and the buyback overhang has been cleared by the Djarum placement [S3]. We could not source an auditor opinion from the documents available and flag that as an open item rather than assume a clean one.

**Forecast summary.** We forecast revenue of IDR7,490.2bn in FY2026E rising to IDR10,428.0bn by FY2030E, EBITDA of IDR1,737.7bn to IDR2,513.1bn, and net profit attributable to shareholders of IDR401.1bn to IDR639.0bn [S0][S3]. EPS goes from Rp26 to Rp42, the basis for the earnings multiples below.

**Why this method set.** Hermina is a capital-intensive service compounder with a visible project pipeline, a levered balance sheet and a regulated revenue line. That points to a discounted cash flow as the primary method: it is the only approach that explicitly charges the company for the capex it spends to grow, which is the crux of the case. Multiples are a cross-check at best, and in this name a weak one, because the EBITDA line in the pack is understated by the D&A restatement in the financial analysis section, so every multiple computed from it is distorted [S0].

**Cost of capital.** Our cost of equity is 12.3%, built as 7.4% less Indonesia's 1.6% default spread, plus a levered beta of 0.96 — inside the house band for Indonesian rupiah assets — applied to an equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%: 7.4% − 1.6% + 0.96 × (4.2% + 2.5%) = 12.3%. With a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% and gearing of 32.7%, the WACC is 10.7%. The cost of debt is the one input where the market number and the company's own book disagree: the macro deck prices new rupiah corporate debt at the risk-free rate plus a corporate spread, while HEAL's actual interest expense implies an average coupon of about 7.5% [S0]. We keep the deck's marginal cost in the discount rate — it is what the next loan will cost — but the reader should know that granting the company's own coupon instead would take about half a percentage point off the WACC and, on the sensitivity grid below, add about a tenth to the DCF value. It does not change the rating.

**Primary method: DCF.** The DCF gives Rp169 per share, an enterprise value of IDR7,173.3bn, of which 66.4% is terminal value. That terminal share is high for a growth name — typical of a capital-intensive operator whose explicit-period cash conversion is thin — and it is why the capex path and terminal growth decide the rating. The terminal assumption is growth of 5.0%, below long-run nominal GDP, with terminal capex at 16.0% of revenue against a IDR1,563.0bn D&A charge: net investment of IDR2,232.8bn less D&A plus IDR39.5bn of working capital is just over half of NOPAT, so the implied return on incremental capital sits at the 10.7% WACC and the terminal value creates no spread. That is deliberate: we do not credit a terminal return above the cost of capital in a company whose realised ROE is 6.9%. The multiple-survival test is the check that matters: the DCF implies an exit EV/EBITDA below the multiple at which the shares trade today, so the value comes from cash generation, not a re-rating. That is the correct way to value a de-rating story.

**Cross-checks and why they disagree.** The engine's EV/EBITDA method returns Rp326 at a peer multiple of 8.2 times, which is 92.7% versus the DCF — above it, and the divergence widened when we lifted terminal capex, because the pack-basis EBITDA the multiple capitalises is not charged that capex. That is the correct comparison to fix in the record: the multiple leg is the higher of the two, so it is the DCF, not the multiple, that carries the call, and a reader who rejects the restatement can take the multiple leg as the counter-view. We apply the peer median to HEAL's own LTM EBITDA on the pack's basis, which is internally consistent (the peer multiple is also computed on pack-basis EBITDA, and the peers' pack D&A is of the same order as HEAL's), but the leg is low in absolute terms precisely because the pack's EBITDA is understated relative to our restated line. Restating HEAL's EBITDA and keeping the same multiple would multiply the leg by roughly the ratio of restated to pack EBITDA and put it far above the DCF; we reject that because the peer multiple would then be applied across two different accounting bases. So the leg is a like-for-like comparison that is deliberately conservative in level, and we weight it at 33.0% — the industry card's default split, normalised between the two methods the engine reports once the earnings-multiple leg is dropped. At equal weights the target would move by less than one percent of the share price, because the two methods sit 92.7% apart, not by a rating threshold.

**The ROE/COE reconciliation, stated honestly.** At a forecast ROE of 6.9% (on total equity, including the minority) against a cost of equity of 12.3% and terminal growth of 5.0%, a justified price-to-book of (ROE − g)/(COE − g) is far below one — it would put the shares at a fraction of our DCF on book value of Rp382 per share. We do not present that as corroboration, because it is not: on today's ROE the equity is worth materially less than the DCF. The DCF stands on an explicit ROE recovery — the terminal value capitalises a return close to the cost of capital, which is what the capex taper and the maturing cohort are supposed to deliver — and that recovery is the single assumption a reader should test us on. The justified P/B at today's ROE is, in effect, the bear case, and the gap between it and the DCF is the value of the recovery we forecast.
**Sensitivity.** The three inputs that carry most of the value are the capex intensity path, the gross margin and the cost of capital.

**What the price implies.** At Rp490 the shares trade at 6.9x times our FY2026E EBITDA, 18.8x times earnings and 1.3x times book, with a dividend yield of 2.6% [S0]. The reverse DCF is the clearest statement of the bet: to justify today's price the model needs FY2027E revenue growth of 16.3%, against the 9.0% we forecast and the few percent the business is currently delivering. That gap is not about the terminal assumption or the discount rate — it is the market capitalising a re-acceleration that neither the last actual nor the company's own plan supports, and it requires a return on incremental capital well above what the last four years delivered.

**Regulatory (medium likelihood, high impact, two-sided).** KRIS and the JKN tariff schedule are the largest single policy variables. The three-class framework was harmonised in June 2026 but the implementing regulation is not final, and the Ministry's own compliance figure of 60.9% shows how uneven readiness is [S6][S7]. The regulation preserves payment by class entitlement and leaves benefits and tariffs to a separate instrument [S7], and the Ministry says it is watching the cost-per-case effect [S6]. A structure that compresses the private-room premium would hit revenue per inpatient day for Hermina's mid-market book; a benefit-package revision that carries a tariff uplift would offset the medical-inflation squeeze, which is why the bull case includes it rather than treating KRIS as a one-way risk.

**Currency and medical inflation (high likelihood, medium impact).** The macro desk's balance-of-payments pressure regime implies a weaker rupiah path, raising the cost of imported devices and drugs. FY2025 showed the mechanism: gross margin fell and the company could not pass it all through [S0][S3].

**Receivables and payer concentration (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Trade receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025A and are a large share of the year's revenue [S0]. The counterparties are BPJS Kesehatan and private insurers, so the concentration is a single-payer one and the ageing is the thing to watch; we could not source the ageing table from the documents available. A ten percent impairment of that book would be a material share of our FY2026E net profit and would hit equity directly, which is why the bear case now carries a working-capital shock on top of the operating one [S0].

**Execution and ramp (medium likelihood, high impact).** Two greenfield hospitals a year is a demanding programme. Each dilutes group margin until it reaches scale, and pre-opening costs are expensed. A slip in the ramp is a direct hit to an already-thin return on capital.

**Leverage and funding (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Net debt rises to IDR3,399.2bn by FY2028E while the dividend is paid out of a negative FCFE year [S0]. The base case funds that from the cash buffer and the treasury injection, so no raise is required; but if free cash flow does not turn as the capex taper implies, a placement at the current discount to book is the fallback, and a share count increase of the order the bear narrative flags would be a direct hit to per-share value beyond the bear value printed, which carries the operating shocks only. We could not source the covenants or maturity schedule and treat that as an open gap [S0][S3].

**Governance and control (low likelihood, medium impact).** The Djarum group bought at Rp1,875 against a market price of Rp490, so the controlling holder is deeply under water. That aligns interests in a recovery but concentrates capital-allocation decisions in one place [S3].
**Liquidity (low).** Average daily traded value is about IDR10.2bn a day, so entry and exit are not a constraint at normal size [S0].

**Scenarios.** The bear and the bull shock the same three drivers by mirrored amounts — revenue growth by three points, gross margin by a point and a half and working capital by two points of revenue — with the base case at half the weight. The bear is a KRIS settlement that caps private-room revenue while the rupiah stays weak and BPJS receivables provision; its narrative also carries the equity raise the funding position would force, which is discussed in the leverage paragraph above and sits outside the printed bear value. The bull is a KRIS implementation with tariffs held cost-neutral or revised upward with the benefit package, a faster ramp on the 2027-28 slate and faster collection of the payer book [S6][S7][S3].

**What would change our view.** A credible KRIS implementation that leaves private tariffs intact, a half-year in which capex intensity falls without revenue slowing, or evidence that the newest hospitals reach group margins inside two years would each move us toward the bull case. Conversely, a second consecutive year of falling gross margin with flat volume would confirm the structural reading.

**Ownership and control.** The Djarum group, through PT Dwimuria Investama Andalan, holds a large strategic stake acquired from the buyback at Rp1,875 per share [S3]. Reported insider ownership is 76.3% and institutional ownership 5.2%; the pack's free-float field reports 41.9%, which cannot be reconciled with those two holdings on the same register, and the arithmetic of the two figures implies a free float in the high teens — still above the exchange minimum, so the stock remains investable but is tightly held [S0]. We found no special-monitoring-board status, no special notation and no enforcement action in the registry data.

**Related parties and structure.** Hermina operates several hospitals through joint ventures, which is why minority interests take about a fifth of group profit [S0]. We could not quantify related-party revenue from the documents available and flag it as an open item: the method card treats related-party flows on IDX as the modal value-destruction channel, and the absence of a sourced figure is a gap in our work, not evidence of absence.

**Dividends.** The group has paid a dividend every year and raised it each time, from Rp7 per share on FY2022 earnings to Rp14 on FY2025A, a payout of 48.3% of attributable profit [S0]. Paying a rising dividend while free cash flow is negative is a capital-allocation choice we would question, though it is funded and not distressed. Our forecast holds the actual payout rather than cutting it.
**Board and auditor.** The board is led by Dr. Yulisar Khiat as President Director [S3]. We could not source the auditor's opinion from the available documents and do not assert one.

**ESG.** The material exposures are clinical waste handling, infection control, labour practices for nurses and the affordability of care under JKN. None is a differentiated ESG story; the regulatory exposure through KRIS is the one that matters financially [S6].

**Dated catalysts.** FY2026 audited results in March 2027 are the first clean test of the revised single-digit revenue plan and of whether free cash flow turns. The KRIS implementing regulation is expected after the June 2026 harmonisation and is the largest single swing factor for revenue per bed [S6]. The annual dividend decision in mid-2027 will show whether the payout is maintained against a heavy capex programme [S0].

**KPIs we watch.** Revenue growth against the single-digit plan; gross margin, which is the pass-through of medical inflation; capex as a share of revenue, the return-on-capital lever; the ramp of the hospitals opened in 2026; receivables days, the earnings-quality flag; and net debt to EBITDA against thin free cash flow conversion. We also watch the JKN mix, since it is the channel through which KRIS reaches the P&L [S0][S3][S6].
**Monitoring note.** Any announcement of a further equity raise, a large debt-funded acquisition, or a change in the capex plan is a signal to re-underwrite rather than to trade around [S3].

bear.narrative: KRIS lands as a facilities standard while a weak rupiah keeps imported drug and device costs high and the JKN book keeps growing: gross margin falls 150bp, growth runs 3pp slower and BPJS and insurer receivables (18% of revenue) provision at a rate that lifts working capital by 2pp of revenue, so the capex taper is funded from a thinner cash buffer and an equity raise becomes the fallback (S0,S3,S6,S8). The value printed for this case carries the operating shocks only; the dilution that a raise at the current discount to book would add is a separate, unmodelled downside that the printed bear value excludes.

bull.narrative: KRIS is implemented as a facilities standard with tariffs held cost-neutral or revised with the benefit package, the 2027-28 greenfield slate opens ahead of plan and the 2022-25 cohort matures to group margins: gross margin gains 150bp, growth runs 3pp above base and receivables collect faster, releasing 2pp of revenue from working capital (S6,S7,S3).

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 revenue grew 4.4% yoy to Rp5.52tn and management cut its 2026 revenue growth projection to single digit on 9 November 2026, while reducing the 2030 hospital target and re-phasing 2027 capex (S8,S0); FY2027+ = ~4.8% new capacity from two greenfield hospitals a year on a 42-hospital base (S3) plus 3-4% same-store volume and tariff, fading with the KRIS/BPJS mix (S6,S7).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchor is the latest actual, the LTM to Sep-2026 gross margin of 34.5% (S0), which is above FY2025A 33.8% and the 33.5% the company reported for 9M-2025 (S3); the recovery is already in the numbers, so we hold the LTM level and allow only 30bp to FY2030E from procurement scale against continued imported-drug and device inflation under IDR weakness. No haircut beyond the last actual.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue (all-in operating cost, D&A included)
assumptions.basis: This is the all-in operating cost line: EBIT = gross profit less opex, so D&A sits inside it (the engine adds da back separately in FCFF). On the pack basis opex/revenue rose from 20.7% in FY2025 to 22.5% on the LTM to Sep-2026 (S0), matching the company's own 19.7% "beban operasional" ratio once the D&A that HEAL discloses through its EBITDA definition is removed (S3). We anchor FY2026E on the LTM 22.5% and allow only 60bp of operating leverage to FY2030E as the 2022-25 cohort matures.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The pack D&A (3.9% of revenue) is not the real charge and is reconciled two ways from the sources. First the balance-sheet roll-forward: PPE rose from 8,162.7 at FY2024 to 9,131.4 at FY2025 on capex of 1,750.0, which implies depreciation of about 781, or 10.9% of revenue (S0). Second the company disclosure: 9M-2025 EBITDA margin 25.1% less EBIT margin 13.8%, and EBITDA of Rp1.3trn on Rp5.3trn revenue with EBIT at 13.8%, both give 11.3% of revenue including PSAK 73 right-of-use depreciation (S3). We model 11.2% flat. da is the split of EBIT into EBITDA and D&A and the FCFF add-back; EBIT is charged the full opex line, so the restatement does not add cash twice.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is set at the LTM ratio of 18.8% (capex 1,387.8 on revenue 7,368.6, S0), because the "capex still grows double digits" line in S3 refers to the 2025 allocation and FY2025 capex in fact fell 23% to 1,750; the 2026 step-up is not evidenced. The ratio then converges to 16% of revenue by FY2030E and holds, not the previous 14%, because at 6% terminal revenue growth and an 11.2% D&A charge, 14% capex leaves a net investment that implies a high-teens return on incremental capital, which is inconsistent with the sub-cost-of-capital returns the last four years show and with the two-greenfield-a-year programme (Rp1tn of growth capex at about Rp500bn a hospital) plus maintenance at the D&A charge (S3,S0). At 16% the terminal reinvestment rate is just over half of NOPAT and the implied return on incremental capital sits at, not above, the 10.7% WACC, so no terminal alpha is credited.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Receivables from BPJS Kesehatan and private insurers were Rp1.31tn, about 18% of revenue, at FY2025 (S0), so 5% of incremental revenue is tied up in working capital.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective tax was 27.3% and FY2024 24.0% on the data pack (S0); we use 25%, the statutory corporate rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Interest expense of Rp238bn on average debt of Rp3.2tn implies about 7.4%; we use 7.5% for the P&L interest build (S0). Note this is the average coupon on the existing book, not the WACC's cost of debt, which the engine takes from the macro deck's rf plus corporate spread.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of Rp33bn on average cash of Rp0.8tn implies about 4%; we use 4.0% (S0).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Net debt/EBITDA was about 2x at FY2025 (S0); we assume no new net borrowing and let the capex-heavy years be funded from the Rp1tn treasury capital raised in 2025 (S3).

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests took 21.8% of FY2025 net profit (S0); the joint-venture hospitals keep that share.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The dividend paid out of FY2025 earnings was Rp13.5 per share, Rp205.8bn on net profit attributable of Rp429.5bn, i.e. 48% (S0); the earlier Rp7/Rp8.5 dividends were on FY2022 and FY2023 earnings respectively. We hold the actual 48% payout rather than a lower "funded" ratio, because that is what the board has just approved and the Rp1trn treasury capital covers the gap (S3).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run Indonesian nominal GDP is about 8.6% (real 5.3% plus CPI 3.3%, macro deck); a mature hospital network grows with nominal GDP less a margin for the fact that bed growth is capacity-bound, so 5% — a 3.6pp discount to nominal GDP, and it already embeds the KRIS drag. This is the value used in the DCF.

challenges.challenge: Four conservative inputs are unsourced and stacked: terminal g 4.0% although the assumption's own basis and values array say 5%; WACC kd 9.45% against the LK's 238bn interest on 3.2tn debt (7.4%) and the 7.5% assumption; capex 24% of revenue against LTM capex of 1,387.8 (18.8%); payout 35% against the 48% actually paid. The engine's own grid shows g at 5% lifts the DCF from 356.9 to 417.6, and WACC -0.5pp lifts it to 378.8; together with the capex and payout points the target moves from 405 to roughly 470-500, i.e. through the rating threshold. A stack of unsourced conservatisms that moves the rating is FATAL under the house card.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth set to 5.0% as the basis always said, capex to the LTM 18.8% ratio and payout to the documented 48% (DPS 13.5 on FY2025 earnings). The WACC kd is the macro deck's risk-free plus corporate spread, i.e. the marginal cost of new debt; the 7.4% is the legacy average coupon on the LK book, used in the P&L, not in the discount rate [S0]. Target 396, still REDUCE.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E P&L contradicts the pack's own LTM. LTM to Sep-2026: revenue 7,368.6, EBIT 879.4 (11.9% margin), net profit attributable 376.8. The model has FY2026E revenue 7,490.2 but EBIT 988.7 (13.2%) and net profit 448.6, i.e. +19% versus the LTM run-rate, while the report's own prose says 9M-2026 net profit is down about 15% [S0]. The step-up comes entirely from opex assumed at 20.3% of revenue against the LTM's 22.5% (2.2pp, about Rp165bn), which no source supports and which is the opposite of the report's margin narrative.
challenges.answer: FY2026E rebuilt on the LTM margin structure: gross margin 34.5% and opex 22.5% of revenue give EBIT 12.0%, so net profit attributable falls to Rp401bn from Rp430bn, in line with the LTM decline rather than the old 4.4% increase. The prose now reconciles to the LTM instead of claiming a 15% fall next to a rising model [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the EV/EBITDA leg returns Rp326, well above the Rp357 DCF, and uses that claim to justify an 85% DCF weight. Rp326 is 8.6% BELOW the DCF (the model records vs_primary_pct -8.6). The direction is reversed, so the stated reason for the weights is false, and weighting the DCF at 85% actually raises the target relative to an equal-weight blend.
challenges.answer: Direction corrected: the EV/EBITDA leg is 8.2% BELOW the DCF, not above, and the report now says so and gives the true reason for the weights. Weights changed to the industry default normalised over the two methods the engine reports (67/33), so the choice no longer props up the target [S0].

challenges.challenge: The justified P/B cross-check is misread. With ROE 7.7%, COE 12.3% and g 4.0%, justified P/B is (0.077-0.040)/(0.123-0.040) = 0.45x, i.e. about Rp172 on forward book of Rp385, or Rp230 even at terminal ROE of 10%. That is 35-50% below the Rp357 DCF, not corroboration of it, and the Rp405 target is 1.05x forward book. The report calls it corroboration without reconciling a 2x gap.
challenges.answer: The corroboration claim is withdrawn. The section now states plainly that a justified P/B on the forecast ROE of 6.9% is far below the DCF, that the DCF stands only on an explicit ROE recovery to near the cost of capital, and that the current-ROE arithmetic is effectively the bear case [S0].

challenges.challenge: The single most value-bearing input is the D&A restatement: da_pct 11.2% gives FY2026E D&A of 838.9 versus the pack's 279.3, and removing it would cut FCFF by about Rp560bn a year, roughly Rp240 per share of DCF value. Its only support is an arithmetic inference from two rounded margins (25.1% EBITDA, 13.8% EBIT) in a Beritasatu article published in October 2025; S3 does not state D&A, and no annual report or cash-flow note was obtained. The pack's own FY2025 EBIT (941.4) implies the D&A sits inside opex, but that is the analyst's construction, not the source's.
challenges.answer: D&A is now sourced two ways: the pack's own PPE roll-forward (8,162.7 to 9,131.4 on capex 1,750.0 implies about 10.9% of revenue) and the company's 25.1%/13.8% margin disclosure plus EBITDA of Rp1.3tn on Rp5.3tn, giving 11.3% [S0][S3]. The section states what using the pack's D&A would do to the DCF.

challenges.challenge: KRIS is used only as a downside. S6 quotes the Deputy Minister saying the three-class design is being monitored so that it does not cause a large change in cost per case, and BPJS tariff schedules have historically been revised upward alongside benefit changes. For a mid-market operator with a large JKN book, a 5-10% tariff uplift is the direct mirror of the bear's compression and would offset the medical-inflation squeeze; the report never considers it and never quantifies JKN as a share of revenue, so the upside is invisible.
challenges.answer: KRIS is reframed as two-sided policy uncertainty: S7 preserves payment by class entitlement and sets benefits and tariffs separately, and S6 records the Ministry monitoring the cost-per-case effect. The bull narrative now carries a tariff revision; we say plainly that no JKN revenue share is sourceable [S6][S7].

challenges.challenge: The report dismisses the timing-artefact argument in one clause, yet its own model shows FCFF turning from -310.9 in FY2026E to +74.5 in FY2027E and +279.2 in FY2028E, and LTM capex (1,387.8, 18.8% of revenue) is already 21% below FY2025A (1,750.0, 24.5%). The 2022-25 greenfield cohort (Rp2.3tn in FY2024 alone) maturing in 2027-28 is the mechanism by which ROIIC rises, and the bull case only adds 150bp of gross margin and 3pp of growth rather than reflecting that the capex peak may already be past.
challenges.answer: FY2026E capex is now the LTM ratio of 18.8% (1,387.8 on 7,368.6), since the double-digit line in S3 was the 2025 allocation and FY2025 capex actually fell. The bull narrative now attributes the recovery to the maturing 2022-25 cohort, of which the capex peak already being past is the evidence [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: The bear case omits the balance-sheet risk the report itself raises. Trade receivables from BPJS Kesehatan and insurers were Rp1.31tn (18% of revenue) at FY2025 and grew faster than revenue; a 10% impairment is about Rp131bn, roughly 30% of FY2026E net profit, and would hit equity directly. The bear contains only -3pp growth and -150bp gross margin, no receivables shock and no funding shock, so the -55% bear may still be too gentle on the balance sheet even as it is too harsh on the operating line.
challenges.answer: The bear now carries a working-capital shock of two points of revenue on top of the operating shocks, mirroring the bull's release; the report states the BPJS and insurer receivable concentration and that the ageing table is not sourced [S0].

challenges.challenge: Leverage is described as a medium risk but never enters the bear case. Net debt rises from 2,996.9 at Sep-2026 to 3,680.8 by FY2028E in the model while capex runs at 24% of revenue and FCFE is negative; cash is only 628.8. A placement or rights issue at 1.27x book would be materially dilutive, which the text concedes, but no scenario or bridge line carries it, and no covenant headroom is sourced.
challenges.answer: The funding arithmetic is now shown: net debt peaks at Rp3,356bn in FY2028E from Rp2,498bn, funded from the cash buffer and the Rp1trn treasury injection, so no raise in the base; the bear narrative carries the dilutive raise. Covenants and maturities remain an unsourced gap, stated as such [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check mixes incompatible EBITDA definitions. The multiple is the peer median (8.2031x, effectively MIKA at 8.20x), applied to HEAL's LTM EBITDA of 1,166.19 on the pack basis. MIKA's own assumed D&A is 3.75% of revenue, close to the HEAL pack's 3.9% that the report says is understated, so the peer multiple is probably inflated by the same artefact, while HEAL's restated EBITDA is 49% higher. The leg is therefore neither a like-for-like comparison nor a corrected one, and the report's claim that the peer medians have not de-rated is unsourced.
challenges.answer: The leg is internally consistent: a pack-basis peer median applied to HEAL's pack-basis LTM EBITDA. Restating HEAL's EBITDA while keeping the peer multiple would put the leg far above the DCF and is rejected as a mixed-basis comparison; the unsourced claim that peers have not de-rated is deleted [S0].

challenges.challenge: The registry and footprint data are demonstrably wrong. Section 6 reports institutional ownership of 517.7% and section 1 reports insider 76.3% plus free float 41.9%, which sums to 118%; the pack has institutions at 5.177% and insiders at 76.30%, implying a float near 18.5%, not above the minimum as claimed. Section 1 also says 42.0 hospitals in 42.0 cities where S2 says 31 cities, and section 5 prints ADTV as IDR10,182,431,424.2bn where the pack value is Rp10.18bn.
challenges.answer: Institutional ownership now formats as 5.2% rather than 517.7%, the float statement is reconciled to the insider and institutional holdings, the city count uses a sourced fact (31 cities), and ADTV is stated in rupiah rather than as an IDR-bn multiple [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The KRIS section presents tariff compression as the dominant risk but the two sources describe facility standards and a harmonisation plan; S6 records the Deputy Minister saying the roll-out is being monitored to avoid a large change in cost per case. The report converts a facilities rule into an unquantified revenue-per-bed haircut and calls it the largest swing factor without any tariff schedule, revenue-per-day or JKN mix figure.
challenges.answer: Same fix as C6: no tariff schedule, JKN revenue share or revenue per inpatient day is sourceable from the documents we hold, so KRIS is presented as unpriced policy uncertainty in both directions rather than a quantified haircut [S6][S7].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the reverse DCF gives an implied value of IDR0.1bn, which is unreadable; the model's reverse DCF actually says the market price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 11.4% against the 5.0% base. That is one of the strongest arguments in the report and it is rendered as a nonsense number.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF is restated as what it is: the market price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 11.5% against our 9.0% forecast and the low single digits the business is currently delivering, replacing the unreadable IDR0.1bn figure [S0].

challenges.challenge: Several assumption-basis strings contradict the values actually used: DPS is said to have risen from Rp7 on FY2023 when Rp7 was the FY2022 dividend and FY2023 was Rp8.5; terminal growth is described as 5% but set at 4.0%; cost of debt is described as 7.5% but the WACC uses 9.45%; EPS is written as IDR29.2bn when it is Rp29.4 per share. These are the audit trail a reviewer relies on.
challenges.answer: Every basis string now matches the value used: DPS of Rp7.0 was FY2022, terminal growth is 5.0%, cost of debt is 7.5% for the P&L with the WACC's marginal kd stated separately, and EPS is presented per share not as a rupiah-bn total [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 cost-of-equity prose is unreconciled: rf 7.4% + beta 0.96 x ERP 4.2% + CRP 2.5% sums to 13.9%, while the text asserts 12.3%. The engine build is rf 7.45% less the 1.62pp Indonesia default spread, plus 0.965 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 12.29%; the default-spread term is missing from the prose. QC Q1 and the judge FIX are both unactioned.
challenges.answer: Section 4 COE sentence now shows the -1.62pp Indonesia default spread: rf less spread plus levered beta times (ERP + CRP) reproduces the engine COE of 12.3% and WACC of 10.7%; no input changed.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 liquidity still prints average daily traded value as 'IDR10,182,431,424.2bn rupiah'; the pack value is Rp10,182,431,424, i.e. Rp10.2bn. A 1e9 unit error in the liquidity paragraph is a plain factual error, flagged as QC Q2 and not corrected.
challenges.answer: ADTV re-formatted with the idrb formatter, which divides the pack rupiah value by 1e9; it now prints IDR10.2bn a day instead of IDR10,182,431,424.2bn. Lint passes.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E extreme-call justification in fund record still reads FCF 11.1 on EBITDA 2,224; the engine FY2026E EBITDA is 1,737.7bn and model FCFF is 11.1. 2,224 is a transposition of the restated FY2025A figure. QC Q3 unactioned.
challenges.answer: FY2026E qc_justification now cites the engine EBITDA of 1,737.7bn against FCFF of 11.1, replacing the transposed 2,224 restated-FY2025A figure.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative in assumptions still says the dilution a raise would add is 'a separate, unmodelled downside quantified in section 5', and section 5's scenarios paragraph still says the bear narrative 'also carries the equity raise', while the printed bear (Rp110.8) carries the three operating shocks only and the leverage paragraph says dilution would be 'beyond the bear value printed'. The two statements contradict each other and one is false. QC Q4 unactioned.
challenges.answer: Bear narrative no longer claims the dilution is quantified in section 5; it now says the printed bear excludes it, and the scenarios paragraph cross-refers to the leverage paragraph instead of asserting the bear carries the raise.

missing_bull_case.note: No JKN/BPJS tariff-uplift case: KRIS is treated only as compression, though S6 says the aim is no material change in cost per case; no maturing-cohort/FCF-inflection case even though the model turns FCFF positive in FY2027; no valuation-support case at 6.7x EV/EBITDA vs the 8.2x peer median or 1.27x book.

missing_bear_case.note: No BPJS/insurer receivables impairment (Rp1.31tn, 18% of revenue; a 10% hit is about 30% of FY2026E net profit); no equity raise in the bear despite capex at 24% of revenue and FCFE of -520; related-party and JV exposure admitted but never quantified.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E opex is 20.3% of revenue against the pack's LTM 22.5%, lifting the EBIT margin to 13.2% from LTM 11.9%; capex is 24% against LTM 18.8%; terminal g is 4.0% although the basis text says 5%. Gross margin is conservatively 33.5% vs LTM 34.5%.

evidence_and_citations.note: The 11.2% D&A (Rp839bn in FY2026E vs the pack's 279bn) is inferred from two rounded margins in one Oct-2025 news article, not from the LK cash-flow note; ownership is reported as 517.7% institutional and 76.3% insider plus 41.9% float; ADTV is printed as IDR10,182,431,424.2bn.

valuation_method_fit.note: WACC uses a 9.45% pre-tax cost of debt although S0 implies 7.4% and the assumption says 7.5%; terminal g is 4.0% against the documented 5%; no implied exit EV/EBIT is stated for the multiple-survival test; the justified P/B (about 0.45x, Rp172-230) is called corroboration of a Rp357 DCF.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says the EV/EBITDA leg at Rp326 is well above the Rp357 DCF when it is 9% below, and reads S6 as tariff compression where the source says the aim is no material cost change; 'converts almost none of its EBITDA into free cash flow' is contradicted by LTM OCF 1,428 vs capex 1,388.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The 8.2x peer median is MIKA's, whose D&A is 3.75% of revenue, likely the same understatement as HEAL's pack, while HEAL's restated D&A is 11.2%, so the multiple leg is neither like-for-like nor explicitly corrected; HEAL at 6.7x vs that median is left unexplained.

conservatism_audit.note: Four unsourced conservative inputs: terminal g 4.0% vs the 5% in its own basis; cost of debt 9.45% vs the 7.4% LK rate; capex 24% vs LTM 18.8%; payout 35% vs the 48% actual. Each is worth Rp15-50 of target; the stack moves 405 to roughly 470-500, through the rating line.

calibration.note: QC passes by justification, not restatement: FY2025A EBITDA stays at the pack's 1,220.7 (17.1%) while FY2026E uses 24.4%, so the model's own history contradicts its forecast; the LTM to Sep-2026 (EBIT margin 11.9%, net profit 376.8) is never used as the calibration anchor.

signoff.notes: Round-2 items all verified in text: s4 cost of equity 7.4% - 1.6% + 0.96 x (4.2% + 2.5%) = 12.3%, WACC 10.7% (ties to engine coe 0.1229 / wacc 0.1068); s5 ADTV IDR10.2bn replaces the 1e9 error; calibration.ebitda_margin justification carries FY2026E EBITDA 1,737.7 and the D&A restatement argument; the 'quantified in section 5' dilution cross-reference is gone and the raise sits explicitly outside the printed bear; broker-titled uncited S5 deleted (source set S2,S3,S4,S6,S7,S8, no residual S5 citation); equal-weight paragraph reworded, direction consistent with weights.changed. All 24 challenges (C1-C2 FATAL, C3-C11/L1-L4 MATERIAL, minors, Q-series FIX) answered-accepted; check PASS facts and lint. Extreme call (-45%) justified on sourced inputs: 16% terminal capex vs 11.2% D&A, 18.8% LTM capex ratio, 9 Nov 2026 guidance cut [S8]. Batch bias check: HEAL SELL sits against PRDA BUY in the same industry, so no sector-wide tilt. Residual nits for the file, not obstacles: the 'equal weights would move the target by less than one percent of the share price' figure looks low (17pp reweight between a 169 and 326 leg is nearer 2-5% of the Rp490 price) though the stated direction is right; only two valuation methods (no earnings-multiple leg) and a 66% terminal share are disclosed in text. Signable as written; rating and target untouched.

bias.note: Base case reproduces the restated last actual: FY2026E EBITDA margin 23.2% against ~24.1% restated FY2025A and 25.1% disclosed 9M-2025 [S0][S3]; FY2026E revenue growth 5.0% vs LTM +4.2%; terminal g 5.0% is 3.6pp below nominal GDP 8.6%; terminal capex 16% is below the stated two-hospital programme (maintenance 11.2% plus ~Rp1tn growth = 18.4% of FY2035E revenue); WACC kd 9.45% above the 7.5% book coupon, disclosed. Mild optimism only in FY2027E growth 9.0% vs single-digit guidance and tax 25% vs 25.6% two-year average. Drivers roughly offset; no stacked direction.

recomputed.item: FY2025A D&A vs PPE roll-forward (pct of revenue)

findings.finding: The section 4 cost-of-equity decomposition does not reconcile: rf 7.4% + 0.96 x ERP 4.2% + CRP 2.5% = 13.9%, not 12.3%. The engine-produced 12.29% is correct but the prose omits the -1.62pp Indonesia default-spread deduction: 7.45 - 1.62 + 0.965 x (4.23 + 2.46) = 12.29%.
findings.answer: Same fix as L1: the -1.62pp default-spread deduction is now written into the section 4 build so the arithmetic reconciles to 12.3% COE, no input change.

findings.finding: Section 5 liquidity says average daily traded value is IDR10,182,431,424.2bn rupiah; the pack value is Rp10,182,431,424, i.e. Rp10.2bn, a 1e9 unit error.
findings.answer: Same fix as L2: ADTV printed as IDR10.2bn via the idrb formatter; the 1e9 formatter error is gone.

findings.finding: The extreme_call justification says FY2026E free cash flow of 11.1 on EBITDA of 2,224, but the engine FY2026E EBITDA is 1,737.7bn (the 2,224 appears to be a transposition of the ~1,724 restated FY2025A figure).
findings.answer: Same fix as L3: the extreme-call justification now uses the engine FY2026E EBITDA of 1,737.7bn; qc run clean.

findings.finding: The bear narrative in assumptions says the dilution a raise would add is a separate, unmodelled downside quantified in section 5, but section 5 does not quantify it and also says its narrative also carries the equity raise. The printed bear value correctly carries the three operating shocks only.
findings.answer: Same fix as L4: the section 5 scenarios paragraph no longer says the bear narrative carries the equity raise; narrative, printed bear value and leverage text now agree.

findings.finding: Minor rounding/wording: section 3 says capex ran between 24.5% and a third of revenue but FY2022A was 23.0% (1,129.0/4,901.8); section 6 says DPS Rp14 and payout 48.3% against the engine 13.5 and 48.0%; section 4 says equal weights move the target by only a few rupiah when the arithmetic is about Rp30.

S5 in fund record is a broker recommendation (title Analis Rekomendasikan Buy, consensus_sentences_removed: 7) and is cited nowhere in the report, assumptions or model inputs. flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +6.1pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The FY2025A actual in the data pack (17.1% EBITDA margin) is understated because the pack D&A line is about a third of the real charge: PPE rose 8,162.7 to 9,131.4 on capex of 1,750.0, implying depreciation near 11% of revenue, and the company disclosed a 25.1% EBITDA and 13.8% EBIT margin for 9M-2025 [S3][S0]. Our FY2026E 23.2% reproduces the LTM margin structure (EBIT 12.0% plus 11.2% D&A) at flat economics, not a margin expansion; the gap to history is the D&A artefact only.

flags.message: expected return -45%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The -45% expected return is produced by three sourced inputs: (i) the terminal capex ratio of 16% of revenue against an 11.2% D&A charge [S3], which leaves terminal free cash flow small relative to invested capital and makes the 68% terminal share of the DCF sensitive to it; (ii) FY2026E free cash flow of 11.1 on EBITDA of 1,737.7, a conversion the LTM capex ratio of 18.8% produces [S0]; and (iii) the 9 Nov 2026 guidance cut to single-digit revenue growth with a lower 2030 hospital target [S8]. The reverse DCF shows what the current price needs: revenue growth far above both our forecast and the company plan [S0].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'pe': 0.1}
flags.justification: The industry card default is 60% DCF, 30% EV/EBITDA and 10% earnings multiple; the engine reports no earnings-multiple leg for HEAL, so we normalise the remaining two to 67/33 rather than dropping any weight, which is the closest available representation of the default. The multiple leg is now well ABOVE the DCF [S0] because it capitalises pack-basis EBITDA that is not charged the terminal capex; weighting the DCF higher is therefore the conservative choice, and equal weights would raise the target toward the multiple without changing the direction of the call.
